nodes.title: Building an analytics assistant so designers and PMs could self-serve
nodes.summary: Brightside's analytics tools were powerful, but most designers and PMs avoided them because they felt too technical. I built a custom GPT that knew our tools, event definitions and data schema, and gave step-by-step instructions for building dashboards and pulling metrics.
nodes.result: The product and design team used it and said they would keep using it. It was an early example of AI changing how we worked, alongside what we built.
answers: Tell me about a time you took initiative.
How do you use AI in your work?
How have you helped your team work more independently?

nodes.title: Coaching a designer to turn incremental work into a long-term vision
nodes.summary: The designer was focused on near-term work, and I helped him see the chance to step up as a strategic design partner.
nodes.result: A long-term vision that aligned the team's roadmap and turned a near-term project into a more complete solution. He was later promoted to lead designer.
answers: Tell me about a time you coached a designer to think more strategically.
How do you help designers grow beyond execution?
How do you keep a motivated designer engaged when the roadmap is incremental?

nodes.title: Testing a shorter signup by deferring medical history
nodes.summary: Brightside's Growth team wanted a shorter signup, but 120 of the 180 intake screens were medical history that therapists needed before a first session. I helped the squad designer set up an experiment with his product team and clinical leaders that moved those questions until after signup.
nodes.result: Conversion rose slightly, which wasn't enough to justify the extra work for therapists, so the change wasn't kept. The pilot built trust with clinical leadership and made later changes easier to explore.
answers: Tell me about an experiment that didn't work.
How do you validate assumptions early?
How do you balance business goals with other stakeholders' needs?

nodes.title: Adding in-the-moment help to Brightside's signup
nodes.summary: Funnel data showed people dropping off at one step of Brightside's signup. Interviews revealed why: many people didn't know the difference between a psychiatrist and a therapist. I led the team that added answers and FAQs right inside the flow at that step.
nodes.result: The pattern spread to other hard decisions in signup, and completion improved by roughly 10 to 15% at the high-friction steps.
answers: How do you use data to inform design?
How do you combine quantitative and qualitative research?
How do you design for complex or high-stakes decisions?

nodes.title: Reframing Brightside's intake around trust, not just conversion
nodes.summary: Brightside's intake had 180 screens and took most people about an hour. The research showed that people seeking mental health care arrived anxious and unsure, and that feeling was a bigger barrier than the screens themselves. I helped reframe the work around trust and built a vision for a modular intake that felt supportive.
nodes.result: The team started asking how to make people feel supported while they signed up. The CEO asked when we could build it, and the vision shaped the Growth team's next roadmap.
answers: Tell me about a time you reframed a problem.
How do you use data and research to set direction?
Tell me about a vision you pitched to leadership.

nodes.title: Redefining velocity with engineering
nodes.summary: Engineering wanted more velocity, while designers were seeing shortcuts and more quality issues. I asked our engineering director what velocity meant to him. It turned out he wanted earlier confidence that work was on track, which designers wanted too.
nodes.result: We tied velocity to shared customer outcomes and made quality a shared principle. Designers stopped raising concerns about shortcuts, and trust between design and engineering grew.
answers: Tell me about a time you disagreed with engineering.
How do you balance speed and quality?
How do you partner with engineering?

nodes.title: Turning a call with a blind user into a privacy-safe research framework
nodes.summary: A blind user raised a question about Brightside's website, so I called him to learn how he used it. Because any follow-up research could expose private health information, the call led me to work with legal on a research waiver and a framework for future studies.
nodes.result: The issues he described went to the team that owned those areas, and Brightside had a privacy-safe way to run research with members going forward.
answers: Describe a time legal pushed back on a design or feature.
How do you work with legal and compliance?
How do you approach accessibility?

nodes.title: Getting buy-in for adaptive search in a finance-driven culture
nodes.role: Director of Product Design, Fulfillment, Search & Ads
nodes.summary: Etsy's search roadmap was full of small optimization experiments with no long-term direction. Using existing research, I made the case for an adaptive search experience that could work differently for jewelry, furniture and gifts. I also worked out a way to free one squad from its near-term revenue target.
nodes.result: Senior leaders aligned, and a squad was dedicated to adaptive search.
answers: Share an example of a challenge you've faced as a design leader.
Tell me about a time you got buy-in for work without a near-term financial return.
How do you balance discovery work with business targets?

nodes.title: Coaching a new manager through a critique conflict
nodes.summary: In a critique, a staff designer gave a junior designer blunt feedback and left her feeling shut down. His manager was new to managing and asked me for help. I coached the manager to address it quickly by naming the behavior, its impact and what to try next time.
nodes.result: The designer took the feedback well, apologized and changed his approach in later critiques. The new manager applied the same approach later on.
answers: Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult situation with a direct report.
How do you give difficult feedback?
How do you support new managers?

nodes.title: Reframing delivery estimates around honest expectations
nodes.summary: Etsy buyers were used to exact delivery dates from Amazon, but sellers ship from home on their own schedules, so engineering couldn't calculate an exact date reliably. I helped the squad shift the question to how we could set honest expectations within those limits.
nodes.result: We shipped a delivery range with plain language about why handmade items take longer, and kept narrowing the range over time.
answers: Tell me about a time engineering constraints changed your approach.
How do you partner with engineering?
Tell me about a time you reframed a problem.

nodes.title: Shifting from day-to-day support to strategic partnership after my scope grew
nodes.role: Director of Product Design, Fulfillment, Search & Ads
nodes.summary: When my scope at Etsy grew from Fulfillment to include Search and Ads, I stayed too focused on day-to-day team needs. My product partner wanted more strategic partnership from me. I added a layer of foresight to how I worked with my partners, picking the highest-impact places where I could help and being selective about where I leaned in.
nodes.result: I spent more time with partners on planning, resourcing and long-term strategy, which led to the adaptive search work. The same feedback didn't come up in my next annual review.
answers: Tell me about a time you failed.
What is an area you are working to grow in?
Tell me about feedback you received and how you acted on it.

nodes.title: Aligning Etsy leadership on a fulfillment vision
nodes.summary: Etsy's fulfillment squads didn't understand the larger strategy, and the industry benchmark was warehouse-speed delivery that independent sellers could never match. I led a three-day workshop where product, engineering, research and business leaders set a shared vision and principles.
nodes.result: Leaders aligned on a vision built on clear, trustworthy delivery expectations. Seven or eight squads used the principles to guide their roadmaps, and our leadership approval score rose in the next engagement survey.
answers: Tell me about a time you created a vision or strategy for your team.
Tell me about a time you aligned senior stakeholders with different priorities.
How do you bring clarity to an ambiguous problem space?

nodes.title: Redesigning Walmart's baby registry in one quarter
nodes.role: Sr. Manager II, Routine Consumables and Baby Registry
nodes.summary: Walmart's redesigned baby registry wasn't working. A chatbot pre-filled each registry, and parents felt it took away the fun of choosing. We had one quarter to fix it. I grew the team from one designer to five, and we went back to the research and gave parents a choice in how much help they got.
nodes.result: Launched on time on iOS, Android and web. Quality registry creations rose 28% year over year, and curation rose 20% against a 10% goal.
answers: How do you drive design forward?
Tell me about a project delivered under a tight deadline.
How do you keep a team motivated under pressure without compromising quality?

nodes.title: Untangling shipping and pickup in Walmart's combined shopping experience
nodes.role: Sr. Manager II, Head of Design for Fulfillment
nodes.summary: When Walmart combined its shipping and grocery experiences, shoppers could add an item and only learn in the cart that it would ship next week instead of arriving with tomorrow's groceries. My Fulfillment design team worked with business partners on the root cause and designed a way for shoppers to see and switch how each item reached them.
nodes.result: The cart design was finished and in development when I left for Etsy, and the source-level fix was still being worked through with business partners.
answers: How do you partner with engineering?
Tell me about a complex design problem you solved.
How do you design across operational and technical constraints?
